I have been a loyal T-Mobile customer since 2016, when they launched the T-Mobile ONE plan. I have been using a military discount for most of that time, but even with the discount, my bill has ballooned to $113 a month thanks to T-Mobile's price hikes. I had finally had enough and started looking for a cheaper alternative. Add in the fact that Apple's iPhone 18 Pro costs at least $100 more this year, and I figured that if I was going to upgrade to a new phone, saving some money on my service could help offset that cost. So, I started looking into MVNOs.

What is an MVNO?

MVNO stands for "Mobile Virtual Network Operator." In short, an MVNO is a wireless carrier that does not own its own nationwide cellular network. Instead, it buys network access from one of the big carriers (like AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon) and resells that service to its customers. Think of them as middlemen for wireless service.

This means that switching to an MVNO doesn't necessarily mean giving up the network you're already using. For example, Mint Mobile uses T-Mobile's network, Visible uses Verizon's, and US Mobile lets customers choose between all three major carriers. In this article, I'll focus on these three MVNOs, as they were the ones I researched most thoroughly before leaving T-Mobile, but there are many other options out there.

Ultimately, MVNOs offer you another way to buy cellular service without going directly to the company that owns the network.

How are MVNOs cheaper? And is there a catch?

If MVNOs use the same cellular networks as AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon, how can they charge so much less? The simple answer is that MVNOs don't bear all the costs of being a nationwide wireless carrier. They don't have to build and maintain their own networks, many operate primarily online without physical stores, and they have fewer employees. These savings can be passed on to customers through lower monthly fees.

MVNO plans tend to be simpler, without a lot of the "perks" and extras you often find with traditional big carriers. Depending on the carrier and plan, you may not get free streaming services or other perks designed to keep you as a customer. But if you really want those "free" things, the money you save by using an MVNO will likely be enough to subscribe to them yourself.

That's my situation. I always looked forward to the free MLB.TV subscription T-Mobile offered and used it every season, but I never watched Netflix, so the "Netflix on Us" perk was a complete waste for me. Even if I wanted both Netflix and MLB.TV, I could pay for them myself and still come out ahead after accounting for the savings from switching. At the end of the day, I just want reliable and affordable cellular service. I don't need a bunch of extras from T-Mobile to justify using them.

The "catch" is less about worse service and more about buying less. What exactly you give up depends on which MVNO and plan you choose. Video streaming may be limited to lower resolutions, the amount of high-speed or premium data you get will vary, and network priority may be different. I have very fast Wi-Fi at home and rarely go to congested places like concerts or sporting events, so network priority isn't a huge concern for me in my day-to-day use. But I do travel internationally occasionally, so international data is an important consideration. Some MVNOs include international data and texting, others charge extra for it, or coverage outside the U.S. may be more limited.

Then there are some less obvious differences, especially when it comes to buying a new iPhone. When you choose an MVNO as your carrier, you can't take advantage of the Apple Card Monthly Installments or the iPhone Upgrade Program. If you want to use either of these options, you're limited to AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon. Practically speaking, this means that if you buy your iPhone directly from Apple, you generally have to pay for it all upfront. The big carriers can also offer large trade-in credits and other promotions that you typically won't find with MVNOs. Apple Watch support isn't available with every MVNO either, so if you have a cellular Apple Watch, you'll want to keep that in mind.

Finally, most MVNOs rely primarily on phone and chat support, rather than face-to-face staff at physical retail locations. I consider myself fairly tech-savvy and have absolutely no desire to stand in line at a store for help. In my experience, the salespeople in stores just call on your behalf and wait on hold with the same people I could call from home, so this is a non-issue for me.

Most importantly, these limitations are not universal across MVNOs. They vary by carrier and plan, so it's worth looking into exactly what you'll be getting before you make the switch.

Three MVNOs worth considering

Once I decided to leave T-Mobile, I started looking for alternatives. Verizon and AT&T's postpaid plans were even more expensive than what I was already paying, so the other two major carriers were out. I ultimately narrowed my search down to US Mobile, Mint Mobile, and Visible. Each had something that appealed to me, and all three could help me significantly lower my monthly bill while still using a major carrier's network.

US Mobile is arguably the most flexible of the three, and it's the one I ultimately switched to from T-Mobile. That doesn't mean it's necessarily the best fit for you, or even the best MVNO of the three. It's just the one that worked best for me.

US Mobile wasn't actually my first choice. I had never heard of the company before I started researching MVNOs. But the more I looked at what they offered, the more I realized they were different from the rest. Here's why: US Mobile offers service on all three major U.S. networks, so customers can pick the one that works best for them. They also have a Multi-Network add-on feature that allows you to activate two networks on the same iPhone (the additional line runs in the background), so when your primary network has poor or weak coverage, your iPhone can switch to the other network (US Mobile describes it as "when coverage is low"). To use this feature, you need to enable "Allow Cellular Data Switching" in the Cellular Data settings on your iPhone. This feature costs extra from US Mobile, and I don't personally need it, but it's a neat option to have.

I had just moved and wanted to see how Verizon's coverage compared to T-Mobile's around my new home, so I decided to test both. I set my wife's iPhone to US Mobile's Light Speed network (which uses T-Mobile), while my iPhone used Warp (which uses Verizon), so we could compare the two networks firsthand. Turns out Verizon was significantly better in our area, so switching to US Mobile ended up being a win-win: better coverage and a much lower monthly bill.

Mint Mobile was originally my top choice because it's owned by T-Mobile, meaning I could stick with the network I was already familiar with but pay a lot less. What I didn't like was that it didn't include international data. My wife and I love taking cruises, and we travel frequently, so having cellular data outside the U.S. is important to us. Mint does offer international data, but it's an add-on, and it would quickly eat into the savings. I also didn't like that taxes and fees were charged separately.

Visible is similarly straightforward, but it only runs on Verizon's network. My biggest hesitation with Visible was Verizon's coverage in my area. I had been a T-Mobile customer for almost a decade and knew the T-Mobile network like the back of my hand, but I had no idea what Verizon's coverage was like. This was actually the only thing holding me back from choosing Visible over US Mobile, since US Mobile lets me try Verizon's network, but if Verizon doesn't work out, I still have T-Mobile and AT&T to choose from. Visible also includes a free cellular Apple Watch line with its top-tier unlimited plan, which is another attractive selling point. (US Mobile offers the same perk on its top-tier plan, as long as you're using its Warp Verizon network.)

What you need to switch

Switching to an MVNO was easier than I expected. My wife and I kept our existing iPhones, and it took about ten minutes to transfer both lines from T-Mobile to US Mobile. I didn't even have to leave the couch. You'll need an unlocked, compatible iPhone (or Android phone, but I'm focusing on iPhone here), along with some information from your current carrier. If you want to keep your phone number, be sure not to cancel your old service until the number has been successfully ported.

Here's what you'll need to make the switch:

  • Your account number with your current carrier
  • Your porting PIN
  • An unlocked, compatible iPhone
  • A new eSIM
  • A little patience

I had already prepaid for two US Mobile unlimited plans for the full year in preparation for the switch. My wife doesn't have a cellular Apple Watch and doesn't care about high video quality, so she opted for US Mobile's Unlimited Starter plan, saving $100 over the Unlimited Premium plan I chose. Two lines plus the Apple Watch plan for a full year came to $500, compared to the $1,356 I was paying T-Mobile for two lines with no Apple Watch service. (Again, that's with the military discount factored in.)

Getting a porting PIN from T-Mobile was a straightforward process—I had expected it to be buried and complicated, but it wasn't. The steps for Verizon and AT&T can be found here.

Once my iPhone was connected to Wi-Fi, US Mobile emailed me a new eSIM, and the installation process was as simple as clicking a button in the email and following the on-screen prompts. My wife's iPhone was exactly the same. The only extra step was setting up my Apple Watch, which I did easily through the US Mobile app.

Why I'll continue using an MVNO

Same network, less money: For the amount I saved, what I gave up was absolutely worth it. I have fast Wi-Fi at home, so cellular data is less critical for me (though in speed tests, US Mobile was just as fast as T-Mobile). For me, the most important thing is having a strong and reliable cellular signal when I'm away from Wi-Fi, especially for making and receiving calls and texts.

No long-term contracts: Most carriers have moved away from traditional contracts in favor of device installment plans, which effectively keep you tied to their network until you've paid off your device. I've always bought my iPhones directly from Apple because I like the freedom of having an unlocked device, but I also appreciate that US Mobile, Mint, and Visible don't require contracts.

Easy to switch: Most MVNOs let you pay month-to-month, so you're never locked into a long-term contract. One month, one carrier might have a good deal; the next month, another might offer something better, and switching is quick and easy. Prepaid accounts don't require credit checks either, so every time a carrier checks your credit report, it won't ding your credit score the way a postpaid account would, and you won't be denied based on your credit history. My credit is fine, but if I decided to switch from T-Mobile to Verizon and they did a hard inquiry, I wouldn't want my credit score to take a hit.

Top comments from Richard Lewis (Rich)

I left AT&T a few years ago and switched to Mint Mobile. It was one of the best tech decisions I've ever made.

Paying for a full year upfront saves more: This kind of flexibility comes at a price, but if you're willing to prepay for a full year of service, you can save even more. Most MVNOs offer significant discounts on annual plans, essentially trading some of the freedom to switch whenever you want for a lower overall price.

No surprise charges: As I mentioned earlier, my wife and I love taking cruises. If you've ever gotten on a ship and forgotten to turn on Airplane mode, only to have your phone connect to the ship's cellular network, you know the nasty surprise of a massive bill. With a prepaid plan, I don't have to worry about accidentally racking up an enormous roaming bill. If international roaming isn't included in the plan, my phone simply won't connect to a foreign network and charge me. US Mobile's plans also include taxes and fees, so the price you see is the price you pay.

I didn't switch to an MVNO simply to find the cheapest service—I wanted to pay for the service I actually want without having to shell out extra for things I don't want or need. So far, I haven't felt like I'm missing out on anything that matters to me (though I know I'll miss that free MLB.TV subscription). In fact, I now have an Apple Watch line I didn't have before, and I'm spending less money. I'm using the same iPhones and the same phone numbers, coverage in my area is better on US Mobile's Warp (Verizon) network, and I have the freedom to switch again in the future if I find something better.

Your priorities may be different from mine, and an MVNO may not be the right choice for everyone. But if you're spending a lot on your current cell service and haven't considered an MVNO, it's absolutely worth a look. You may be surprised at how little you actually have to give up.
